doc.title: Hal Espinosa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 20, 2024

title: Technology and the union: Monk's question on the virtual orchestra
summary: Monk asks about technology and Local 47; Hal recalls the virtual orchestra as the issue.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: You know we talk about — especially people with gear — oh Jeez, this gig is on the second floor, I’ve got to carry my keyboards up and all that stuff, and they didn’t feed the band. And when I hear that description I just said yup, that’s something to remember. I want to talk about music, musicians and technology for a bit. And it’s connected to your role in the musicians’ union. I came across this historical musical fact the other day and it said in 1927 the first talkie, “The Jazz Singer” was released, displacing orchestras in movie theaters. The AF of M had its first encounter with wholesale unemployment brought about by technology. 22,000 theater jobs for musicians who accompanied silent movies were lost while only a few hundred jobs for musicians performing on soundtracks were created by the new technology. And this kind of thing has followed music since then. When you became president of the professional Musicians’ Local 47 what was the main concern at that time with technology and working musicians?

Well at that time it went to — all these terms I’m kind of losing from my memory you know because I’ve been away from it for well I stepped down from office in 2009 so what’s that 15 years ago? But they had the —
It’s not a synthesizer but it’s similar to it where there’s a keyboard player down there playing a whole score.
